slide.title: Is Every Claim Supported?
slide.body: Answer sentences on the left, source chunks on the right; teal lines join supported claims; one unsupported claim in amber. Small tag: RAG Systems · Lesson 12.

scenes.on_screen_text: One sentence the chunk never said
scenes.voiceover: Retrieval found the right chunk. The model wrote a fluent answer with two citations. But one sentence says something the chunk never said. Retrieval metrics cannot see this problem. You need to check the answer itself.

slide.title: Measuring Answer Quality
slide.body: RAG Systems · Lesson 12 of 16 · Faithfulness and relevance

scenes.voiceover: In the last lesson, we measured retrieval. Today we measure the answers, with two metrics that matter most in RAG.

slide.title: Two answer metrics
slide.body: Faithfulness: every claim supported by the chunks · Answer relevance: fully addresses the question · Unanswerable questions: correct refusal rate

scenes.voiceover: Faithfulness means every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved chunks. An answer can be true in the real world, and still be unfaithful, if it adds facts the context does not contain. Answer relevance means the answer addresses the question that was asked, completely. And for unanswerable questions, we score correct refusals separately.

slide.title: Judge verdict
slide.body: { "faithful": "yes" | "partly" | "no", "unsupported_claims": [ … ], "relevant": 1–3 } · rubric: use only the CHUNKS, no outside knowledge

scenes.voiceover: Checking every answer by hand is slow, so we ask a model to act as a judge. It gets the question, the chunks and the answer, plus a clear rubric, and returns a structured verdict: faithful yes, partly or no, a list of unsupported claims, and a relevance score from one to three. The judge never sees the expected answer.

scenes.stock_query: teacher marking exam papers at desk
scenes.on_screen_text: Check the marker before trusting marks
scenes.voiceover: Think of a new teaching assistant who marks exam papers with a marking guide. The assistant is fast. But before you trust their marks, the lead teacher marks a sample of the same papers. If they mostly agree, and the differences make sense, the assistant can mark the rest.

screen_steps: Show the judge and human label lists for five answers.
Run print(rate, diffs) and show the exact output 0.8 [(1, 'yes', 'partly')].
scenes.voiceover: So a judge must be checked. This small function compares the judge's labels with yours. In the example with five answers, agreement is zero point eight, and there is one difference, on the second answer. The judge said yes, and the human said partly. Read every disagreement like this one.

screen_steps: Run the pipeline over 25 test questions.
Open answers.jsonl and show one saved line with question, chunks and answer.
scenes.voiceover: Now a real evaluation. Kwame is a developer for an agricultural advice service in Kumasi, Ghana. Extension officers ask about crop guidance. He runs twenty-five test questions, twenty answerable and five unanswerable, and saves the question, chunks and answer for each one to a file.

screen_steps: Show JUDGE_RUBRIC and the judge call with a structured verdict.
Run it over the 20 answerable answers and save the verdicts.
Show his own labels for 10 answers in a separate file, created before opening the verdicts.
scenes.voiceover: For the twenty answerable ones, he calls the judge with his rubric, and saves the verdicts. You'll see something like a list of verdicts, each with a faithfulness label and any unsupported claims. Before he opens that file, he labels ten answers himself.

screen_steps: Run agreement and show 8 of 10 with two disagreements.
Open one disagreement and highlight the planting month missing from the chunks.
Edit the rubric to 'list every claim first, then check each claim', re-judge, and show 9 of 10.
scenes.voiceover: Agreement is eight of ten. In both differences, the judge said yes, but the answer added a planting month that was not in the chunks. He changes the rubric: list every claim first, then check each one. He judges again, and agreement rises to nine of ten.

slide.title: Kwame's results (hypothetical)
slide.body: Faithfulness bar: 16 yes · 3 partly · 1 no. Correct refusals: 4 of 5. Pattern: gaps filled with general knowledge → stronger 'only from the chunks' rule.

scenes.voiceover: His example results: sixteen of twenty faithful, three partly and one not faithful, and four of five correct refusals. The unfaithful answers share a pattern. The model filled gaps with general farming knowledge, so he strengthens the only from the chunks instruction.

The model API is paid, so keep evaluation small. Use your test set, not thousands of questions. Save answers so you can judge again without generating again. For larger runs, consider batch processing.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Faithfulness, relevance, refusals. 2. Judge = rubric + structured verdict + human check. 3. Small sets, saved outputs, batch runs.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, faithfulness checks that every claim is supported by the retrieved chunks, answer relevance checks that the answer addresses the question, and refusals are scored separately. Second, a model judge needs a clear rubric and a structured output, and must be checked against your own labels. Third, keep evaluation cheap with small sets, saved outputs and batches.
